title: How does multi-level caching (L1 local in-memory like Caffeine in front of L2 Redis) absorb a stampede burst: when Redis expires a key, each instance briefly serves it from L1 so only one request per instance reloads: and what is the consistency trade-off (short L1 TTL = less stale, longer L1 TTL = stronger DB protection)?
shortTitle: How does multi-level caching absorb a stampede burst?
keyPoints: Multi-level caching layers per-process Caffeine (L1) in front of shared Redis (L2) in front of the database.
A read flows L1, then L2 on miss, then DB on L2 miss, populating upward on return.
When a Redis key expires, each instance still has the value in L1, so only one request per instance (not per request) reloads.
Caffeine's loading cache provides single-flight: many threads in one instance miss the same key, only one loads.
Short L1 TTL means less staleness but weaker stampede protection; long L1 TTL gives strong protection but more staleness.
For prompt cross-instance invalidation, publish an eviction message over Redis Pub/Sub so each instance clears its L1.
L1 must be bounded with a maximum size and eviction policy to prevent unbounded heap growth.

s1_definition.oneliner: Multi-level caching puts a per-process Caffeine L1 in front of a shared Redis L2, so when a L2 key expires each instance keeps serving from L1 and only one request per instance reloads, with the L1 TTL tuning the trade-off between freshness and database protection.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **L1 (Caffeine)** – a small, fast, in-process cache with nanosecond lookups; scope is one JVM instance, not shared across instances.
- **L2 (Redis)** – a shared distributed cache accessed over the network; all instances read and write the same entries.
- **Stampede Absorption** – when L2 expires, L1 keeps serving per-instance, cutting reloads from "one per request" to "one per instance per L1 TTL window."
- **Single-Flight** – Caffeine's loading cache ensures only one thread per instance performs the reload; others wait for its result.
- **L1 TTL Trade-off** – short L1 TTL = instances re-check L2 sooner (less stale) but fall through more often (weaker protection); long L1 TTL = stronger protection but more staleness.
- **Broadcast Invalidation** – Redis Pub/Sub or a message topic to evict L1 entries across all instances immediately on write.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India the authoritative rate book is in the vault (database), a shared whiteboard in the central hall holds the current rate (Redis, L2), and each teller keeps a sticky note at their window (Caffeine, L1). When the whiteboard gets wiped, each teller still has their sticky note for a little while, so only one runner per window goes to refresh, not one per customer. How long the sticky note stays valid is the trade-off: short note life means fresh figures but more vault trips; long note life means the vault is bothered less but figures can be stale.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Multi-level caching layers per-process Caffeine (L1) in front of shared Redis (L2) in front of the database. The key benefit is stampede absorption: when a Redis key expires, each instance still has the value in L1, so reads continue from L1 without touching Redis or the database. Only one request per instance falls through to reload, cutting database hits from thousands to a handful.

The consistency trade-off is governed by the L1 TTL. A short L1 TTL means instances re-check Redis sooner for less staleness, but fall through more often for weaker protection. A long L1 TTL gives strong database protection but more staleness. For prompt cross-instance freshness, add broadcast invalidation over Redis Pub/Sub.

L1 must be bounded with a maximum size and eviction policy to prevent unbounded heap growth. The layers can use different patterns: L1 as refresh-ahead to never block, L2 as cache-aside with single-flight. A burst is progressively filtered: L1 absorbs most per instance, L2 absorbs most of what gets through, and the database sees only a trickle.

Remember one sentence: layer a bounded Caffeine L1 in front of shared Redis L2 so that when L2 expires, each instance serves from L1 and the database sees one reload per instance, not one per request.
